opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Every time I come back, I'm honestly struck by how fast things change. I left China quite a while ago, and the gap between visits used to feel like a few years' worth of change. Now it feels like a decade can happen in a year or two.

The most noticeable thing is how much convenience is built into daily life. You can go a whole day without touching cash or a card. You scan a QR code for breakfast, a bike, or the subway. Food delivery shows up in twenty or thirty minutes, and it's not just food, it's groceries, medicine, almost anything. When I go back to the Bay Area after a trip, I notice those little frictions again.

As a robotics person, I also pay attention to the physical side of it. You see delivery robots in hotels bringing things up to your room. Restaurants have serving robots. In some cities there are robotaxis on the road and autonomous delivery vehicles. A lot of it is still early and not perfect, but what impresses me is how willing people are to try these things. People are fairly tolerant of new technology in public spaces, and that makes deploying and iterating much faster. For robotics, real-world deployment and data really matter, so that kind of environment is valuable.

On urban development, the infrastructure is remarkable. High-speed rail has changed how people think about distance. A city a few hundred kilometers away now feels like a day trip. The new districts, the subway lines, the airports, the scale is hard to grasp until you see it.

I also try to keep a balanced view. Fast growth brings its own pressures. People work very hard, competition is intense, and young people especially feel a lot of stress around jobs and housing. Some newer areas feel a bit empty, and you wonder whether the pace of building always matches real demand. And older neighborhoods, the alleys and small shops I remember from childhood, are disappearing in some places. That's a bit nostalgic for me.

Overall, though, my main feeling is energy. There's a sense that things are moving and people are hungry to build, and as someone working on embodied AI, I find that exciting. Many of the hardware supply chains and manufacturing capabilities robotics relies on are right there, so it's a very interesting place to watch over the next few years.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, every time I go back, the thing that hits me first isn't anything grand, it's the small frictions that have just disappeared. You land, you turn on your phone, and within an hour you've paid for a taxi, ordered food, unlocked a shared bike, and booked a train ticket, all from one or two apps. I live abroad now, and the contrast is striking. In the US I still carry a wallet. In Shenzhen or Hangzhou I genuinely forget I own one.

But what I find more interesting than the convenience is how it's changed the texture of daily life. Delivery is so cheap and fast that a lot of people, especially younger ones, have basically outsourced errands. You see fewer people in grocery stores and more couriers on electric scooters than cars in some neighborhoods. It's efficient, but I do wonder what gets lost. Some of the street-level life that made Chinese cities feel so alive, the small vendors, the chatting at the market, is thinning out in the newer districts. The older neighborhoods still have it, and people clearly crave it, which is why you see this wave of "city walk" culture and old-town revival.

On the urban development side, I think we're past the era of pure expansion. Ten or fifteen years ago it was all about building new districts, new towers, new ring roads. Now the conversation is about quality: metro lines that actually connect, parks along rivers that used to be industrial, cities like Chengdu or Changsha marketing themselves on livability rather than GDP. The infrastructure is extraordinary. High-speed rail has effectively made the Yangtze Delta or the Greater Bay Area feel like one metro region.

The tension I notice is that the physical city has gotten much better while people's mood is more uncertain. Housing prices, the job market for young graduates, the pressure around "involution," all of that sits underneath the shiny surface. So my overall read is a country that has solved a lot of the hardware problems of urban life and is now wrestling with the software, the question of what a good life in these cities actually looks like.

astra-6.text:
What strikes me is how closely urban development is tied to the small details of everyday life. A new train line matters because it changes someone’s commute; a neighborhood renovation matters because it changes where people shop, walk, and spend time together.

I’d be careful about drawing one conclusion about all of China, though. The experience can vary enormously between cities, and even between neighborhoods. For me, the interesting question is how much that development improves daily life: whether people can get around easily, afford to stay in their communities, and enjoy the public spaces around them.

sol-6.1.text:
What struck me on my recent visits was how much urban development shows up in ordinary routines—how people get to work, shop, and spend time in their neighborhoods. But I’d be careful about treating China as one uniform experience. Even within a city, a new commercial district and an older residential neighborhood can feel very different.

For me, the interesting question is whether development makes everyday life easier. Can people get where they need to go? Can they afford to stay in their neighborhood? Are there places to sit, walk, and meet friends? Those things tell you as much about a city’s progress as its skyline does.
